 Dr. Ahmed Mahmoud Al-Shuraida, a researcher in agricultural heritage in the Arab East, said that the month of November, which corresponds to the eleventh month of the Gregorian calendar, is known in the Arab East as “Tishrin al-Thani,” while it is known in the Arab Gulf countries, Yemen, the Nile Valley and the Arab Maghreb as “November.”
 Why is the month of November called by this name? 
 Al-Shuraida explained that the name “Tishreen” goes back to the Aramaic Syriac Eastern calendar, noting that the word means “beginning” in Arabic, in reference to the beginning of autumn.
 He added that the name of November in the Syriac language is “Tishrin Trayono”, which means the next or second November, and the number of days in this month is 30 days.
 November... the olive harvest season and changing weather conditions 
 November is considered one of the important months in the agricultural heritage of the Arab Levant, as it coincides with the harvest season of the blessed olive tree and the production of olive oil, which is considered one of the finest types of oils in terms of quality.
 This month is also known as a transitional period that witnesses a change in weather conditions, with increased chances of rainfall and the beginning of the region being affected by cold weather.
 The rainy season in November... a bountiful season awaited by farmers 
 Al-Shuraida pointed out that the early clouds that appear during the month of November are known in popular heritage as “Al-Marabi’a”, while the rainy season that comes in the middle of the month, coinciding with the rising of the Pleiades star in the evening, is considered one of the best rainy seasons.
 This season is also known as “Al-Wasam Al-Thurayawi,” due to its coinciding with the appearance of the Pleiades in the sky. It is of great importance to farmers and Bedouin people, as its rains come after a long period of relative drought during the summer and autumn seasons, when the land is in dire need of rainwater.
 According to popular agricultural tradition, rainfall during the period from November 10 to 20 is a promising indicator of a bountiful and fertile season, which explains the optimism that accompanies this period among farmers and Bedouin people.
 The most famous proverbs associated with the month of November 
 The month of November is associated with many proverbs and folk tales passed down in the Levant and the Arab East, reflecting the ancestors' experience in observing weather changes and agricultural seasons, most notably:
 “November is reliable when it comes to rain”: This refers to the fluctuating weather conditions and the irregularity of rainfall during the month.
 “Betsharin, bitukr al-hayaya wa al-haridin”: This is a metaphor for reptiles and animals beginning to hide in their dens as the cold intensifies.
 “The second day of November, the stones get cold and the trees get cold”: a popular expression describing the beginning of the feeling of cold weather and the effect of seasonal changes on trees.
 "The yellowing came and left the trees bare": This refers to the falling and yellowing of leaves as winter approaches. The proverb is also associated with a bird known as "Abu Safir" (the whistler), as the popular saying goes, "Abu Safir whistled and good fortune came," indicating optimism about the arrival of the rainy season.
 “O moon of October, shine upon us and do not make us forget the nights of longing”: This is one of the popular sayings passed down through generations that reflects people’s connection to the atmosphere of October and its memories.
 Thus, November holds a special place in the agricultural and popular memory of the Arab Levant, as it is the month of olive harvesting, anticipation of rain, and the beginning of weather changes that pave the way for the arrival of winter.
